entries.title: The flawed theory of control (Storr)
entries.content: Will Storr (The Science of Storytelling): every protagonist runs on a flawed theory of control — a deep, usually unconscious belief about how to keep the world safe and themselves worthy. The story's events attack precisely this theory. The dramatic question is never 'what happens?' but 'who is this person, really, when their model of reality breaks?' Find the character's flawed theory first; plot is just the machine that tests it.

entries.title: The misbelief and its origin scene (Cron)
entries.content: Lisa Cron (Story Genius): a protagonist enters carrying a misbelief — a specific wrong conclusion drawn from a concrete past moment ('I trusted, and was destroyed, therefore I must never need anyone'). The external plot matters only insofar as it forces this internal misbelief to the surface and demands it change. Build the origin scene of the misbelief before building the plot; the 'third rail' running through the whole story is the protagonist's internal struggle against it.

entries.title: The Lie the Character Believes (Weiland)
entries.content: K.M. Weiland (Creating Character Arcs): the engine of a change arc is the Lie the Character Believes — a false value the protagonist clings to because it once protected them. The Want is what the Lie tells them to chase; the Need is the Truth that would set them free. The arc is the slow, costly trade of the comforting Lie for the painful Truth.

entries.title: Positive, flat, and negative arcs (Weiland)
entries.content: Weiland's arc taxonomy: Positive Change (the protagonist overcomes the Lie), Flat (already holds the Truth and changes the world around them), and three Negative arcs — Disillusionment (learns a bitter truth and is broken by it), Fall (clings to the Lie into ruin), Corruption (sees the Truth and rejects it for the Lie). Choose the arc deliberately; melancholy most often lives in the Disillusionment and Flat arcs.

entries.title: Desire vs psychological vs moral need (Truby)
entries.content: John Truby (The Anatomy of Story): separate the psychological need (what the hero must overcome internally) from the moral need (how they must stop hurting others) from the desire (the concrete external goal that drives the plot). Desire gives the story momentum; need gives it meaning. They must pull against each other — getting what you want should threaten what you need.

entries.title: The ghost — the wound from the past (Truby)
entries.content: Truby's 'ghost' is the event from the past that still haunts the hero — the open wound that froze them into their current weakness. It need not be dramatized in flashback; it's the gravity well bending every present choice. A story without a ghost has a hero with no reason to resist change.

entries.title: Theme as a moral argument (Truby)
entries.content: Truby: theme is not a statement, it's an argument the whole story conducts. The hero pursues a goal by certain means; the opponents pursue the same goal by different means; the structure dramatizes which way of living is better. Don't state the theme — let characters embody competing answers and let consequence render the verdict.

entries.title: Four-corner opposition (Truby)
entries.content: Truby's four-corner opposition: the strongest antagonist wants the same goal as the hero and attacks the hero's greatest weakness. Surround the hero with multiple opponents (not just one villain), each embodying a different value-stance on the central moral question, so conflict comes from every direction and the theme is argued from all sides.

entries.title: The self-revelation at the climax (Truby)
entries.content: Truby: the climax is the hero's self-revelation — the moment they finally see the truth about themselves and their moral failing. It must be earned by the whole arc, surprising yet inevitable, and ideally double: a psychological revelation (who I am) and a moral one (how I've wronged others). A plot climax with no self-revelation is spectacle without meaning.

entries.title: Micro-tension on every page (Maass)
entries.content: Donald Maass (The Fire in Fiction): tension is not reserved for big plot turns — every page needs micro-tension, moment-to-moment uncertainty usually rooted in conflicting emotions inside a single character. Readers don't put books down at the action scenes; they drift during calm pages that forgot to make them feel two things at once.

entries.title: Engineer the reader's feeling, don't report it (Maass)
entries.content: Donald Maass (The Emotional Craft of Fiction): don't report what the character feels — engineer what the reader feels, which is often different. Withhold the obvious emotional label; show the oblique physical or behavioral detail and let the reader supply the feeling. The strongest emotional moments are inferred, not announced.

entries.title: Escalation and therefore/but causality (Saunders)
entries.content: George Saunders (A Swim in a Pond in the Rain): a story is a system of escalation — each unit must raise the stakes or deepen the meaning, never merely repeat. Test causality with 'therefore/but,' never 'and then': events should follow as consequence, not sequence. Saunders' revision rule: read as the reader would, mark where attention dips, and cut or charge that spot.

entries.title: Specificity is meaning (Saunders/Baxter)
entries.content: Saunders and Baxter: specificity is meaning. A 'dog' is nothing; 'the three-legged retriever that still tries to scratch with the missing leg' carries theme, pathos, and character in one stroke. Choose details that do double duty — concrete on the surface, thematic underneath. Vagueness is the enemy of feeling.

entries.title: Yearning at the white-hot center (Butler)
entries.content: Robert Olen Butler (From Where You Dream): at the white-hot center of every living character is yearning — not an intellectual goal but a deep, often inarticulate longing. Plot is the dynamics of desire. If you can't name what the character yearns for (beneath what they say they want), the character isn't alive yet. Write from their moment-to-moment sensory experience, not from your ideas about them.

entries.title: The art of subtext (Baxter)
entries.content: Charles Baxter (The Art of Subtext): meaning lives below the spoken surface. Characters rarely say what they most mean; staging, silence, the half-gesture, and the wrong subject carry the real freight. Build scenes where the spoken text and the emotional undertext diverge — the gap between them is where the reader leans in.

entries.title: Rhyming action and motif (Baxter)
entries.content: Baxter (Burning Down the House): rhyming action — events, images, and gestures that echo across a story accumulate meaning through recurrence. A motif planted early and varied later makes a story feel composed rather than reported. Repetition-with-difference is how prose creates resonance without ever stating its themes.

entries.title: Promise, progress, payoff (Sanderson)
entries.content: Brandon Sanderson: every story makes promises to the reader (tone, central conflict, the kind of payoff coming), shows visible progress toward them, then pays them off in a way both expected and surprising. Reader satisfaction is largely promises kept by an unforeseen route. Audit the opening: what is it promising, and does the ending honor that exact promise?

entries.title: Yes-but / no-and try-fail cycles (Sanderson)
entries.content: Sanderson's try-fail cycles: a plot advances through attempts that go 'No, and things get worse' or 'Yes, but at a new cost.' Straight success is boring; straight failure is static. The yes-but / no-and rhythm keeps progress real while complications compound, and earns the eventual victory or defeat.

entries.title: Limitations beat powers (Sanderson's First Law)
entries.content: Sanderson's First Law, applied broadly: a power's story value comes from its limitations, not its scope. What a character, system, or world cannot do generates more tension than what it can. When building any capability — magic, technology, status, talent — define the cost and the boundary first; that's where the drama lives.

entries.title: The five commandments of a working scene (Coyne)
entries.content: Shawn Coyne (The Story Grid): every scene that works contains five movements — inciting incident, progressive complication (turning point), crisis (a genuine dilemma: a best-bad-choice or two irreconcilable goods), climax (the choice acted on), resolution. And every working scene turns a value (life→death, love→hate, freedom→captivity). If the value hasn't shifted by the scene's end, it isn't a scene yet — it's setup.

entries.title: Genre conventions and obligatory scenes (Coyne)
entries.content: Story Grid: every genre carries conventions and obligatory scenes the audience came for — skip them and you break the reader's contract; deliver them freshly and you satisfy without cliche. Identify the story's controlling genre early, list what that genre obligates, then subvert deliberately rather than by accident.

entries.title: The global value on a spectrum (Coyne)
entries.content: Story Grid: a story tracks one global value on a spectrum (justice↔tyranny, connection↔isolation, meaning↔nihilism). Beginning, middle, and end should mark distinct points on that spectrum, and the climax delivers the value at its most extreme. Knowing the global value tells you what every scene is ultimately measuring.

entries.title: The five-act fractal (Yorke)
entries.content: John Yorke (Into the Woods): structure is fractal — the five-act shape (status quo / inciting incident / midpoint reversal / crisis / climax) repeats inside each act and even each scene. The midpoint is where the protagonist stops reacting and acts, via a moment of truth. Yorke's core insight: protagonist and antagonist usually want the same thing; structure is the externalized shape of internal change.

entries.title: The antagonist as mirror (Yorke/Truby)
entries.content: Yorke and Truby: the most resonant antagonist is the protagonist's mirror — wanting the same thing, or showing what the protagonist could become. The opponent externalizes the road not taken. Design the antagonist as a distorted reflection, not an unrelated obstacle, and the conflict becomes the protagonist arguing with themselves.

entries.title: Craft is cultural, not universal (Salesses)
entries.content: Matthew Salesses (Craft in the Real World): 'craft' rules are not universal laws — they encode the expectations of a particular audience and tradition. 'Relatable,' 'likable,' 'show don't tell,' even three-act structure are culturally specific contracts. Ask consciously whose expectations this story serves, and which conventions to honor, bend, or refuse. Default rules are choices, not physics.

entries.title: Narrative shapes beyond the arc (Alison)
entries.content: Jane Alison (Meander, Spiral, Explode): the dramatic arc is not the only narrative shape. Stories can move as a wave (rising/falling rhythms), a meander (a digressive river), a spiral (returning to the same point transformed), a radial/network (linked cells around a center), or a fractal. For interiority, memory, and melancholy these organic patterns often serve better than the conflict-staircase.

entries.title: Kishotenketsu — structure without conflict
entries.content: Kishotenketsu (ki-sho-ten-ketsu): a four-movement structure — introduction, development, twist, reconciliation — that generates meaning without central conflict. The 'ten' (twist) is a new element or perspective that recontextualizes what came before, not an antagonist to defeat. Ideal for quiet, contemplative, character-driven, or melancholic stories where Western conflict-structure would feel forced.

entries.title: Melancholy as craft: mono no aware / wabi-sabi
entries.content: Mono no aware and wabi-sabi as working tools, not just aesthetics: pathos arises from the awareness of transience — beauty heightened because it cannot last. To build a melancholic register, let joy and loss occupy the same moment: the reunion shadowed by the parting, the bloom already wilting. The ache lives in making the reader feel time passing through the characters.

entries.title: Scene and sequel for pacing (Swain/Butcher)
entries.content: Dwight Swain, popularized by Jim Butcher: alternate 'scenes' (goal → conflict → disaster) with 'sequels' (reaction → dilemma → decision). Scenes drive action; sequels let the character and reader process emotionally and choose the next goal, controlling pace. Skipping sequels makes a story breathless and emotionally flat; over-long sequels stall it. Pace by tuning the ratio.

entries.title: Free indirect style and narrative distance (Wood)
entries.content: James Wood (How Fiction Works): free indirect style lets narration take on the character's idiom and bias without quotation — 'the world's a mess, isn't it' rendered as the narrator's voice colored by the character's mind. It collapses the distance between reader and character. Decide how close the narration sits to the protagonist's consciousness; that choice governs intimacy and irony alike.

entries.title: The telling detail / thisness (Wood)
entries.content: Wood: the telling detail — a single concrete particular ('thisness') that makes a person or place irreducibly real and implies far more than it states. One precise, slightly irregular detail outperforms a paragraph of description. Pick the detail that reveals character or theme sideways, not the one that merely catalogs appearance.

entries.title: Distrust thought verbs (Palahniuk)
entries.content: Chuck Palahniuk (Consider This): distrust 'thought' verbs — knew, realized, understood, felt, wanted, remembered. They summarize and hold the reader at arm's length. Instead 'record' the physical, behavioral, sensory evidence and let the reader assemble the inner state. 'Show don't tell' made mechanical: convert abstraction into observable action and detail.

entries.title: Likability, proactivity, competence
entries.content: The three sliders of character appeal (Sanderson, from screenwriting craft): readers bond through likability (kindness, humor, being wronged — the 'save the cat' beat), proactivity (making decisions and driving the plot rather than reacting), and competence (being good at something). A character low on all three feels inert; raising any one buys engagement. Tune them per role — an arc may begin with a passive hero precisely so proactivity can grow.

entries.title: Compelling characters are built on contradiction (Storr)
entries.content: Will Storr: compelling characters are built on contradiction — the gap between self-image and behavior, the value they preach versus the one they live. We are drawn to people who don't add up, then read on to resolve them. Give the protagonist at least one trait at war with another; consistency is for the dead.

entries.title: Surprising yet inevitable endings
entries.content: The test of an ending (where Saunders, Truby, and Sanderson converge): surprising yet, in retrospect, inevitable. It should answer the dramatic question the opening posed, deliver the self-revelation the arc demanded, and honor the promises made — while arriving by a route the reader didn't predict. If readers can guess it, it's too small; if it feels arbitrary, it wasn't seeded. Earn it through setup, then turn the expected outcome.

entries.title: Inner stakes, not just outer (Maass)
entries.content: Stakes answer 'so what?' — and they must be personal, not just plot-scale. Maass: raise inner stakes (identity, belief, relationship) alongside outer ones; a world-ending threat means nothing if we don't first fear for one specific heart. Establish early what the protagonist stands to lose that the reader has been made to value, then keep threatening exactly that.

entries.title: Make the familiar strange (defamiliarization)
entries.content: Defamiliarization (Shklovsky, kept alive in Saunders and Baxter): art renews perception by making the habitual strange — describing the ordinary as if seen for the first time, slowing the reader's eye. Combat cliche not by reaching for the exotic but by looking harder at the familiar until its strangeness returns. This is how a worn premise becomes singular.

entries.title: The midpoint hinge
entries.content: The midpoint (Save the Cat / Yorke / Story Grid): the center of the story is a hinge — a false victory that curdles, or a false defeat that secretly empowers — and the moment the protagonist shifts from reacting to acting. It cures the sagging middle by reframing the whole goal. Place a genuine point-of-no-return at the halfway mark and the second half gains urgency.

entries.title: Change is cyclical, not linear
entries.content: Real change is cyclical, not linear (Weiland, Cron, and recovery psychology agree): characters encounter the truth, flinch from it, retreat into the lie, suffer consequence, and circle back — each loop a little closer. Decide how many cycles this character needs before the final confrontation breaks the pattern, what specifically breaks it each time, and what is different about the last loop. Instant epiphanies feel cheap; earned ones are paid for in repeated failure.
